clinicalPearls: Presents as slowly enlarging annular or polycyclic erythematous lesions that spread centrifugally with central clearing, favouring the trunk and proximal limbs
A trailing scale on the inner edge of the advancing border is characteristic of the superficial type
It is a reactive figurate erythema and often a marker of an underlying trigger rather than a primary disease
Recognised triggers include infections (dermatophytes, viruses, bacteria), drugs, foods and, less commonly, underlying malignancy
The superficial form is often mildly itchy with the classic trailing scale, whereas the deep form is indurated, non-scaling and more sharply defined
Biopsy of the superficial type shows a tight ('coat-sleeve') perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis
Management focuses on identifying and treating the underlying cause; the eruption often settles once the trigger is removed
reference.pathophysiology: Erythema annulare centrifugum is regarded as a hypersensitivity reaction pattern in which the skin responds to a variety of antigenic stimuli, such as microbial antigens, drugs or, occasionally, tumour-associated antigens. The reactive process produces a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis; the superficial variant additionally shows spongiosis and parakeratosis accounting for the trailing scale, while the deep variant has a denser, deeper infiltrate without epidermal change. Centrifugal spread with central clearing gives the characteristic annular and polycyclic configurations.
additionalInvestigations: Skin scrapings and mycology to exclude dermatophyte infection
Skin biopsy to confirm the reaction pattern and exclude mimics
Screening for infective and drug triggers guided by history
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Age-appropriate malignancy screen if lesions are persistent or atypical
Autoantibody testing where lupus is a consideration
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or atypical lesions raising concern for erythema gyratum repens and internal malignancy
Persistent eruption unresponsive to treatment of obvious triggers
Systemic symptoms suggesting an underlying serious illness
Features overlapping with subacute cutaneous lupus
reference.prognosis: The course is variable, from lesions clearing within weeks to a chronic relapsing pattern lasting months or years; prognosis largely reflects the identifiable underlying trigger, and the eruption often resolves once that is addressed.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for tinea and not confirming with mycology, or vice versa
Failing to distinguish it from erythema gyratum repens, which prompts a malignancy search
Overlooking a drug or infective trigger
Assuming an underlying malignancy in every case, when most are idiopathic or reactive to benign triggers
management: Identification and treatment of the underlying trigger, since the eruption is reactive and often resolves once a driving infection, drug, food or occult malignancy is addressed
Topical antifungal treatment where a dermatophyte infection is demonstrated on scrapings
Topical corticosteroids for symptomatic relief of the itchy superficial form
Oral antihistamines and emollients to control pruritus and skin dryness
Age-appropriate malignancy screening where lesions are persistent, atypical or recur without an obvious cause
Reassurance and observation, recognising the benign and frequently self-limiting course
